claims.text: Systematic non-equiatomic composition adjustment is a method for tuning the magnetic and magnetocaloric behavior of FeCoNiTi-based HEAs.
Increasing Ti content fosters antiferromagnetic coupling in FeCoNiTi-based HEAs.
Additional Ti produces stronger antiferromagnetic coupling with Fe, Co, and Ni atoms.
Increasing Ti content reduces saturation magnetization.
Increasing Ti content enhances magnetocrystalline anisotropy in the fcc phase.
Ti enrichment increases coercivity by enhancing intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
Ti enrichment modifies magnetic-domain structure and domain stability.
Changes in exchange interactions and domain stability shift the magnetic ordering temperatures.
The Ti-induced magnetic changes enhance the magnetocaloric response by making the field-induced entropy change more favorable near shifted transition temperatures.
As-cast FeCoNiTi can contain fcc and C14 Laves phases associated with multiple ferromagnetic transitions.
FeCoNiTi exhibits ferromagnetic transitions at approximately 1084 K, 214 K, and 168 K.
The fcc phase is responsible for the transitions at 1084 K and 168 K, while the C14 Laves phase is responsible for the transition at 214 K.
The fcc phase of as-cast FeCoNiTi has a high coercive field.
The cited baseline is specifically a non-equiatomic FeCoNiTi alloy exhibiting all three listed transitions.
As-cast FeCoNiTi samples can be prepared by arc melting under argon followed by rapid quenching.
Rapid quenching or controlled thermal treatment can maintain a single phase or a selected multiphase microstructure during Ti enrichment.
Broad-temperature magnetic measurements can capture the multiple magnetic transitions of FeCoNiTi.
The proposed tuning effect requires suppression of phase segregation and undesirable secondary-phase formation.
Excessive Ti addition may move the alloy into a regime dominated by other magnetic or structural phenomena.
